title: Joy in the morning (Psalm 30)
hook: weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm twenty-seven: the Lord is my light, and false witnesses closing in. Your line was one thing I ask. Did you come back to your one thing? Day four hundred eighteen.

Three in the morning, wide awake. Lying there with a fever. Sitting in a waiting room as the clock crawls past three. The night after a breakup, or bad news, or a fight you can't take back. Things weigh more in the dark. Worries grow teeth. And then, sometimes without anything at all being fixed, the window goes gray, then pale, and a bird starts up outside, and the same problem looks different in daylight. Not solved. Just survivable. Psalm thirty puts that whole stretch of night into a single line.
screen: `AWAKE PAST THREE.` → `WORRIES GROW TEETH IN THE DARK.` → `THEN THE WINDOW GOES GRAY.`

segments.voice: Psalm thirty, in the King James Bible: "For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." The Hebrew picture is even more vivid. The word for endure, yalin, means to lodge, to spend the night. Weeping comes in like an overnight guest. It's allowed in. It stays the night. But it doesn't move in. In the morning, joy arrives, and the guest leaves. The psalm is a thank-you, and it tells a story. The writer says that when things were going well, he got comfortable. "In my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved." Then God hid his face, he says, and he was troubled. He fell ill, or nearly died; he talks about going down to the pit. He cried out. And he was healed. And then the line about dancing: "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness." Sackcloth was the rough cloth people wore in grief. God, the psalm says, took it off him like a parent changing a child's clothes, and dressed him in joy. The heading calls it a song at the dedication of the house, which the King James reads as the house of David; readers differ on which house is meant. In Jewish prayer books it's said each morning, and at Hanukkah, the feast of the temple's rededication. Some churches read it in the Easter season. The psalm doesn't say the night isn't real. It says the night isn't permanent.
screen: `WEEPING STAYS THE NIGHT, LIKE A GUEST.` · `I SAID, I SHALL NEVER BE MOVED.` · `MOURNING TURNED INTO DANCING.` · `THE NIGHT IS NOT PERMANENT.` · then, large: `WEEPING MAY ENDURE FOR A NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the morning light. If it's morning where you are, look at it now: where it falls in the room, its color, how it moves. If it's later, find whatever light there is, a lamp, a window, a screen dimmed low, and picture tomorrow's first light coming. Settle, and breathe. Think of one night in your life that felt endless, and that ended. You got through it. Let yourself feel that. If you're in a long night now, you don't have to feel joy yet. Just remember that mornings come. If you pray, you can give thanks for one morning. The bell holds the time.
Yalin. Hebrew for lodges, spends the night: how weeping stays like an overnight guest, before joy arrives and the guest leaves in the morning.
Your line: joy comes in the morning. Tomorrow, before you check anything, look at the first light for ten seconds. Day four hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Some churches read Psalm 30 in the Easter season, Christians pray it in times of recovery and thanksgiving, and its line 'joy cometh in the morning' is said at funerals and bedsides.

original.note: Hebrew: lodges, spends the night. Weeping comes in the evening like an overnight guest.

trapdoor: what you thought: cheer up, it'll be fine.
what it means: a thank-you from someone who went through the night, admitting it was real, and singing that it ended.
what a scholar hears: yalin, 'lodges'; a heading about dedicating a house; and the psalm's place in Jewish morning prayer and at Hanukkah.

notes: Editor review (y2 days 407–424): hook no longer opens "Everybody knows" (telling the listener what they know) and drops the hospital image used on days 416 and 423 and the superlative "one of the best-known lines"; "the line that makes people dance" flattened; heading line now notes the KJV reads "the house of David" while readers differ on which house; Jewish use stated as prayer-book custom; cut unsourced "Christians have long prayed it at Easter"; howItsDone "often" removed.
Yalin from lun, 'to lodge, spend the night': standard lexicon. Confirm.
Psalm 30 in Jewish liturgy: recited near the start of the morning service (before Pesukei dezimra) in many rites, and associated with Hanukkah. Confirm the phrase 'opens the morning psalms'.
Now 'some churches read it in the Easter season' (used in some lectionaries in Eastertide); confirm.
'Like a parent changing a child's clothes' is an image for 30:11, not a textual claim.
